title: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation

paper.title: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently . This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher’s quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively , and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M M factorized components tied by a single shared latent . Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M M . We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M = 1 M{=}1 . The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1 × 2.1\times to 3.3 × 3.3\times over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M M , and at M = 8 M{=}8 , it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models now rival autoregressive language models, as they fill every position of a sequence in parallel rather than one token at a time ( Potaptchik et al. 2026 ) . To keep a single denoising step cheap, they factorize the per-step transition across positions, p t → s ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) = ∏ i = 1 L p i ​ ( x s i ∣ x t ) , p_{t\to s}(x_{s}\mid x_{t})\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{i}(x_{s}^{i}\mid x_{t}), (1) and decide every token independently given the current sequence x t x_{t} ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) . This independence is what makes a step cheap, and it is also what makes few-step generation challenging when the target couples positions that must be decided together. If a sentence pairs a subject with a verb that must agree in number, or an opening bracket with its closing match, the correct tokens are correlated, and an independent update commits to them separately. A factorized step may match the individual token marginals, while assigning substantial probability to jointly inconsistent combinations, and additional denoising steps may therefore be needed to resolve the mismatch. Conditioned on k k , the positions remain independent, but each component concentrates on a consistent completion. Marginalizing k k preserves the same per-position marginals as in (a), while placing all joint mass on the agreement set. Thus, two rank-one components express the correlated completion in one transition. Currently, two model families dominate this trade-off. Likelihood models such as MDLM ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) and SEDD ( Lou et al. 2023 ) train a strong factorized denoiser from scratch and then spend many steps at inference, where the factorization assumption is least harmful. Few-step accelerators take a trained teacher and compress its many-step behaviour into a handful of steps, either by distillation (Di4C ( Hayakawa et al. 2024 ) , SDTT ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre 2025 ) ) or by coupling rectification (ReDi ( Yoo et al. 2026 ) ). Both methods are effective, but they inherit the teacher’s quality ceiling. It is well understood that a student cannot outrun the teacher it imitates ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) , and rectification degrades after a few rounds. Hence, neither family removes the factorization at its root. We ask whether correlated steps can be modeled natively without a teacher. Our answer is Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), whose finite-time kernel is a mixture of M M factorized components selected by a latent k ∈ [ M ] k\in[M] : Ψ t → s θ ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) = ∑ k = 1 M w k θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) ​ ∏ i = 1 L P i θ ​ ( x s i ∣ x t , k , t , s ) . \Psi^{\theta}_{t\to s}(x_{s}\mid x_{t})=\sum_{k=1}^{M}w^{\theta}_{k}(x_{t},t,s)\prod_{i=1}^{L}P^{\theta}_{i}(x_{s}^{i}\mid x_{t},k,t,s). (2) Conditioned on ( x t , t , s ) (x_{t},t,s) , we first sample k ∼ w ( ⋅ ∣ x t , t , s ) k\sim w(\cdot\mid x_{t},t,s) , and we then sample the coordinates of X s X_{s} independently given k k . Thus, k k couples positions after marginalization, while each component remains factorized. At M = 1 M{=}1 , LKF reduces to MDLM. This mechanism produces a teacher-free few-step gain. On the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks, the mixture learns heterogeneous components, and a best-of- M M decode that ranks those components by the model’s own likelihood turns them into a few-step gain. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We introduce a latent-kernel discrete flow-map (LKF) whose step is a mixture of M M factorized components tied by one shared latent. 2. We give an exact information decomposition of the correlation a rank- M M step can carry, turning the question of whether the latent captures correlation into two bounded, estimator-validated quantities. 3. We test LKF on synthetic datasets with closed-form total correlation (TC). A hidden-agreement dataset shows that the captured information and the held-out likelihood grow monotonically with M M , while a parity control shows that the latent provably cannot help. 4. We evaluate unconditional generation on the LM1B and WikiText-103 benchmarks against likelihood and accelerator models. At M = 8 M{=}8 , LKF improves few-step generative perplexity by roughly 3 × 3\times over the likelihood baselines and surpasses the distilled and rectified accelerators without using any teacher, with the gain growing with M M .

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Masked diffusion as likelihood models. Building on the absorbing D3PM process ( Austin et al. 2021 ) , MDLM ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) shows that the absorbing evidence lower bound (ELBO) reduces to a weighted cross-entropy on masked positions under the SUBS parameterization, which zeroes the mask probability and copies revealed tokens through, and SEDD ( Lou et al. 2023 ) reaches comparable likelihoods by learning discrete score ratios for a continuous-time Markov chain ( Campbell et al. 2022 ) . Both are factorized per step, where a rate changes one coordinate at a time in SEDD, and the reverse kernel is a product over positions in MDLM. Hence, both need many evaluations before the sample quality saturates. LKF reduces to MDLM as its M = 1 M{=}1 special case (Proposition 4 ) by adding intra-step correlation. Few-step generation by distillation and rectification. SDTT ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre 2025 ) self-distills a masked model through time, and Di4C ( Hayakawa et al. 2024 ) distills into a mixture-of-products student, proving that factorized students face a Θ ⁡ ( 1 / J ) \Theta(1/J) total-variation floor. Hence, both methods are structurally teacher-bounded. ReDi ( Yoo et al. 2026 ) instead rectifies the source-to-target coupling, provably decreasing the same conditional total correlation per round, but its gains ride on a monotone entropy collapse. LKF asks the complementary question, whether the mixture structure can be trained from scratch with no teacher ceiling, enriching the kernel until the correlation is representable. Flow maps and from-scratch few-step models. Flow maps learn a finite-time transition kernel indexed by two times, where one network serves every step. Building on the discrete flow matching family ( Gat et al. 2024 ; Campbell et al. 2024 ) , Discrete Flow Maps ( Potaptchik et al. 2026 ) are the closest from-scratch sibling that carries correlation through position-dependent simplex schedules, but with no latent and no mixture. Concurrent theory quantifies the schedule-level tradeoff between total correlation and step count ( Dmitriev et al. 2026 ; Zhao and Cai 2026 ) , complementing our per-step accounting. LKF is a likelihood model and differs by making each jump a low-rank mixture of discrete-token kernels whose latent is explicit and measurable, a mechanism orthogonal to simplex schedules.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries and background
sections.text: Setup. We model sequences x = ( x 1 , … , x L ) x=(x^{1},\dots,x^{L}) whose tokens take one of V V values from a vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , and corrupted sequences additionally use an absorbing symbol [MASK] ∉ 𝒱 \texttt{[MASK]}\notin\mathcal{V} . Data come from an unknown p data p_{\text{data}} accessed only through samples, and we pursue both generation and density evaluation on held-out data. Superscripts index positions ( x i x^{i} ), and subscripts index time ( x t x_{t} ), with all notations collected in Appendix A . Samples are generated by iterative denoising ( Austin et al. 2021 ) . Starting from all- [MASK] , a learned transition removes a little corruption per step, where each step is one network forward pass (NFE). Masked diffusion. A monotone schedule κ t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \kappa_{t}\in[0,1] keeps each token independently with probability κ t \kappa_{t} and otherwise replaces it by [MASK] ( Austin et al. 2021 ) (Eq. ( 4 )). Masking is also called absorbing, where the reverse process turns [MASK] into real tokens. A denoiser takes the whole partially masked sequence and predicts a categorical over its clean value for each masked position, factorized across positions as in Eq. ( 1 ). MDLM ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) and absorbing SEDD ( Lou et al. 2023 ) are such examples. The endpoint coupling is trivial ( δ [MASK] ⊗ p data \delta_{\texttt{[MASK]}}\otimes p_{\text{data}} ), and the only modelling freedom left is therefore the order and grouping in which positions are revealed, which the LKF latent parameterizes. Factorization is also what forces many steps. Correlated positions revealed in the same step are sampled independently and frequently disagree, and the process can repair the inconsistency only by revealing them in many steps. Flow maps. Discrete flow and diffusion models come in two flavours. Rate-based models (such as SEDD and CTMC discrete diffusion ( Campbell et al. 2022 ) ) learn an instantaneous transition rate and integrate it with a fine discretization at inference. Flow-map models learn a finite-time kernel Ψ t → s θ ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) \Psi^{\theta}_{t\to s}(x_{s}\mid x_{t}) that jumps from t t to s s directly, building on the discrete flow matching family ( Gat et al. 2024 ; Campbell et al. 2024 ) . LKF is a flow-map model, and MDLM is its special case with one component (Proposition 4 , Appendix B ). Total correlation. Correlation is measured by the total correlation (TC) of a joint distribution over the L L positions, TC ⁡ ( X ) = ∑ i = 1 L H ⁡ ( X i ) − H ⁡ ( X ) ≥ 0 , \mathrm{TC}(X)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathrm{H}(X^{i})\;-\;\mathrm{H}(X)\;\geq\;0, (3) the amount by which the joint exceeds the product of its marginals. It vanishes when the positions are independent, and it is precisely what a factorized model discards. Why kernels and not rates. Mixing several factorized rate matrices does not buy correlation. Convex combinations of coordinatewise CTMC generators are again coordinatewise, so the mixed chain still changes one coordinate at a time and its short-time kernel is factorized to O ⁡ ( ε 2 ) O(\varepsilon^{2}) (Proposition 5 , Appendix D.1 ). Correlated transitions exist only in discrete-time kernels or flow maps, which is why LKF is defined as a mixture kernel (Eq. ( 2 )) rather than a mixture of rates.

sections.text: A mixture router has two potential failure modes, and the regularizer guards against both, ℛ = − λ ent ​ H ​ ( 𝔼 b ​ [ w ] ) + λ lb ​ 𝔼 b ​ [ H ⁡ ( w ∣ x t ) ] , \mathcal{R}\;=\;-\,\lambda_{\text{ent}}\,\mathrm{H}(\mathbb{E}_{b}[w])\;+\;\lambda_{\text{lb}}\,\mathbb{E}_{b}\big[\mathrm{H}(w\mid x_{t})\big], (8) where 𝔼 b \mathbb{E}_{b} averages over a batch. sections.heading: 4.4 Inference
sections.text: Sampling starts from the all- [MASK] sequence and applies J J steps with t j = j J t_{j}=\frac{j}{J} and t j + 1 = j + 1 J t_{j+1}=\frac{j+1}{J} . Each step forwards the trunk once, samples tokens at the currently masked positions from a single component k k under the analytic (cached) reverse update, and keeps already-revealed tokens fixed because masking is monotone (pseudocode in Appendix C ). Any residual [MASK] after J J steps is filled greedily. Since the latent is tied to a whole sequence, a rollout draws k k once at the all- [MASK] start, where w w is a constant prior, and holds it for the entire trajectory. Every step is therefore explained by the same latent, and the decode matches the sequence-level semantics of the training objective. One such rollout uses a single component and therefore leaves the mixture’s heterogeneity unused. Our decode, best-of- M M , realizes that heterogeneity at inference by running all M M rollouts in parallel with one component frozen in each, scoring every finished candidate with the model’s own sequence-level mixture negative ELBO (NELBO) of Eq. 16 , and returning the argmin (Algorithm 2 in Appendix C ). The model’s own likelihood is used for selection, which needs no reward model, no external judge, and no teacher, and the M M rollouts are independent and therefore run concurrently at the sequential depth of a single chain. The scoring passes can in fact be reduced. Every step evaluates all M M components in order to marginalize over k k , which makes the log-probability that component k k assigns to the tokens revealed at that step available at no extra cost, and accumulating it along a trajectory gives a per-component running evidence by the time the rollout finishes. Selecting on this quantity is free and is at least as accurate as the Monte-Carlo NELBO. Since it ranks candidates before they finish, it also lets the weakest rollouts be pruned partway through, cutting the cost of best-of- M M by roughly a factor of three.

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate LKF in two settings: language modeling benchmarks LM1B ( Chelba et al. 2013 ) and WikiText-103 ( Merity et al. 2016 ) , and a synthetic corpora.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: LM1B uses the bert-base-uncased vocabulary ( Devlin et al. 2019 ) ( V = 30522 V{=}30522 ) and WikiText-103 uses the GPT-2 byte-pair vocabulary ( Radford et al. 2019 ) ( V = 50257 V{=}50257 ) at a sequence length of 128 128 . These models were trained for 200 ​ k 200\text{k} optimizer steps at a batch size of 512.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We report generative perplexity (gen-PPL) under a GPT-2-large judge ( Radford et al. 2019 ) ( 512 512 samples, decoded and retokenized), swept over NFE ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } \mathrm{NFE}\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} and reported together with the sample entropy, since the judge rewards low-entropy text and perplexity alone can misrank methods. We add ELBO-perplexity (ELBO-PPL) for the likelihood models, which is the exponential of the per-token NELBO.

sections.heading: 6.2 Language modeling
sections.text: We validate LKF on natural language by training it at M ∈ { 1 , 4 , 8 } M\in\{1,4,8\} against the factorized baselines (MDLM, SEDD) and the few-step accelerators (SDTT, Di4C, ReDi) on the LM1B and WikiText-103 datasets, together with an autoregressive transformer (AR) on LM1B. Figure 3: Generative perplexity (PPL) versus number of sampling steps on LM1B, comparing LKF at M = { 1 , 4 , 8 } M{=}\{1,4,8\} against the baseline methods. Figure 4: Illustration of correlation and information captured by LKF on synthetic corpora. On hidden agreement , the captured information I ^ k \widehat{\mathrm{I}}_{k} and the effective total correlation TC ^ \widehat{\mathrm{TC}} rise monotonically with M M , tracking their ceilings ( log ⁡ M \log M and ( L − 1 ) ​ log ⁡ M (L-1)\log M , dashed), and held-out NLL falls accordingly. On parity , every captured-correlation metric stays at zero for all M M .

sections.heading: LM1B
sections.text: Adding mixture components improves few-step generation on LM1B, and the improvement grows with the number of components, as shown in Table 1 and Figure 3 . The eight-component model reaches the lowest (best) generative perplexity of 105 105 at 32 32 evaluations, and it does so with a higher sample entropy than the baselines (sample texts in Appendix H ). The gains also come from how the sampling budget is spent rather than from spending more of it. We also retrained an autoregressive model (a causal transformer) under similar training conditions. Its full-context factorization gives the lowest clean likelihood of any model, with validation perplexity 27.61 27.61 against MDLM’s 33.96 33.96 and our M = 1 M{=}1 base at 34.22 34.22 , but its generative perplexity is 135 135 at a fixed 128 128 function evaluations, one per token, and it therefore cannot enter the few-step regime. The two are not directly comparable, since best-of- 8 8 spends M M rollouts to reach 105 105 but has a sequential depth of 32 32 steps rather than AR’s 128 128 , which makes it cheaper in latency and more expensive in total evaluations. LKF therefore wins on judged sample quality wherever the budget can be spent in parallel.

sections.heading: WikiText-103
sections.text: We repeat the evaluation on WikiText-103 by only changing the corpus and its GPT-2 vocabulary. The single-component LKF again matches the retrained MDLM and edges ahead of both factorized baselines with the lowest ELBO-perplexity. The mixture rows replicate and strengthen the LM1B pattern on this second corpus. At M = 4 M{=}4 , the mixture is live at I ⁡ ( k ) = 0.87 \mathrm{I}(k){=}0.87 nats and reaches 102 102 at 32 32 evaluations, more than 2 × 2\times below both baselines, and widening to M = 8 M{=}8 continues the trend on both axes, raising the captured information to I ⁡ ( k ) = 1.41 \mathrm{I}(k){=}1.41 nats and taking the corpus to 75 75 , which is 3.0 × 3.0\times below MDLM and 3.3 × 3.3\times below SEDD. The likelihood cost of the mixture is not monotone in M M . Moving from one component to four trades ELBO-perplexity 27.89 27.89 for 29.79 29.79 , but the eight-component model recovers most of that to 28.56 28.56 , and the wider mixture therefore buys its generation gain almost for free in likelihood terms. The two factorized models have unigram entropies of 4.33 4.33 (MDLM) and 4.36 4.36 (SEDD) at 32 32 evaluations, well below LKF ( 5.25 5.25 ).

sections.heading: Comparison with few-step accelerators
sections.text: We run two few-step samplers from a trained teacher, namely ReDi from the DUO base ( Sahoo et al. 2025 ) and Di4C from a seven-round SDTT student (the round-by-round results are in Appendix E.2 Tables 4 and 5 ). The two behave differently from one another. ReDi holds the single-evaluation end with a nearly flat curve, but it earns its per-round gains through a steady entropy collapse that the GPT-2 judge rewards as fidelity. Both models stop improving around their fifth round, and because generative perplexity alone misranks them, we also compute their entropy. As shown in Table 1 , the distilled students remain ahead in the ultra-few-step regime, since they inherit a converged teacher’s calibration where the from-scratch mixture’s cold-start low-NFE points are weakest. The ordering reverses beyond roughly eight evaluations. LKF overtakes the SDTT teacher and, at 32 32 evaluations, reaches the lowest perplexity of any row ( 105 105 ), passing both the distilled and the rectified accelerators without using any teacher. ReDi’s low few-step numbers are not directly comparable, since they carry the entropy-collapse failure mode noted above.

sections.heading: 6.3 Synthetic corpora with known correlation
sections.text: We built two synthetic corpora on which the TC is known in closed form and trained LKF on them at M ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } M\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} . The first is hidden agreement , whose joint is exactly representable by a rank- M M mixture, and the second is parity , whose representation cost is exponential in the sequence length. The two theorems make opposite predictions on these corpora, and both predictions hold (Figure 4 ). On hidden agreement, the mixture uses the latent, and uses it more as M M grows, where the captured information rises from 0 0 to 2.46 2.46 nats ( 89 % 89\% of the log ⁡ 16 \log 16 ceiling) and the effective total correlation from 0 0 to 17.1 17.1 nats, both under their ceilings log ⁡ M \log M and ( L − 1 ) ​ log ⁡ M (L-1)\log M , while held-out NLL falls from 3.50 3.50 to 2.56 2.56 nats. On parity, the latent stays off at every M M , with captured information and total correlation pinned at zero and the NLL flat, as the hardness result of Theorem 2 predicts. The full experiments on the captured correlation and the router-mode analysis are in Appendix G .

sections.heading: 6.4 Ablations
sections.text: We freeze the trained LKF model and vary how the latent is selected and used at inference (full details in Appendix F ).

sections.heading: The gain is a mixture property, and it grows with M M .
sections.text: We used the same selector and the judge to isolate the effect of best-of- M M policy, and varied only where the candidates come from. Replacing the M M components by M M noise draws of one component costs 16 % 16\% at M = 4 M{=}4 ( 157 157 against 186 186 ) and 35 % 35\% at M = 8 M{=}8 ( 106 106 against 163 163 ). Eight i.i.d. chains reranked by their own likelihood at the identical budget were also given to the trained MDLM baseline and to our architecture-matched M = 1 M{=}1 model. The reranking helps them substantially, taking them from 363 363 to 199 199 and from 327 327 to 183 183 at 32 32 steps, but the mixture still reaches 106 106 at the same 8 ​ ( J + T ) 8(J{+}T) calls, which is a 47 % 47\% and a 42 % 42\% advantage that widens monotonically from 14 % 14\% at four steps. The components therefore provide a candidate diversity, and that advantage grows as the mixture grows (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: The selector is native, and the cheap version is the better one.
sections.text: Our experiments show that the ranking of the components matters, since a random pick from the same pool gives 327 327 at M = 8 M{=}8 , while every scored pick lands between 106 106 and 163 163 . Selection here uses only the model’s own sequence likelihood, with no reward model, no external judge, and no temperature tuning. The Monte-Carlo mixture NELBO can be replaced with the running evidence that the trunk already produces during generation, which reaches 125 125 against 131 131 at M = 8 M{=}8 , while removing the M ​ T MT scoring passes. The same ordering holds at every step, where the running evidence matches or beats the Monte-Carlo selector at a strictly lower cost. We nonetheless report Table 1 with the Monte-Carlo selector, which is the conservative choice. The candidates can also be pruned mid-trajectory, because the evidence is available at every step. Successive halving reaches 145 145 for 96 96 calls at M = 8 M{=}8 , which is three times cheaper than full best-of- 8 8 for an 11 % 11\% higher perplexity.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: We note two main limitations of LKF. The first is that the single-step exactness is capped by the per-step factorization. Each step is factorized given ( x t , k ) (x_{t},k) , and one disagreeing token can therefore push a sample off support independently of M M , which only smaller steps or a richer per-step structure would remove. The second is that the learned router is not very informative along sampling trajectories. Making the router track component quality would turn best-of- M M into a cheaper single-rollout policy.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented LKF, a discrete flow map whose finite-time kernel is a mixture of M M factorized components, which expresses correlated steps natively and without a teacher. We provided the theory to support it and conducted experiments on the LM1B and WikiText-103 datasets that give the best few-step generative perplexity among the baseline methods.

sections.heading: Architecture equivalence detail.
sections.text: The full-match trunk reproduces the native MDLM backbone rather than only the smaller matched trunk: hidden 768 768 , 12 12 heads, 12 12 blocks, dropout 0.1 0.1 with MDLM’s placement, untied biased output head, a moving average with the same decay and warmup, and MDLM’s block internals (a biased GELU MLP, weight-only LayerNorm, and the standard adaLN conditioning). At M = 1 M{=}1 , the router and latent embedding receive identically zero gradient (a log-softmax over a single logit is identically zero and the regularizers vanish). The residual differences are direction-neutral or fall on the LKF side. LKF feeds the real noise level through the same conditioning pathway that must later carry the latent, which is strictly more information than MDLM’s constant conditioning. The latent blocks also use a small non-zero adaLN initialization for the M > 1 M>1 symmetry break, and the data order differs by seed.

sections.heading: Appendix F Decoding-policy ablations
sections.text: A mixture step is only worth its extra components if something at inference time chooses among them, and we take that claim apart in four steps. We first attribute the best-of- M M gain to the mixture itself rather than to the generic reranking that decodes it. We then ask whether any single-rollout policy recovers the same gain, and since none of them does, some form of selection is necessary. That necessary selection is then made free, after which we turn to the components that the selection chooses among. Every policy is previewed at a single operating point in Table 6 , and the later tables expand the ones that matter over the step grid and across the two corpora.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Unless stated otherwise, every cell uses the LM1B models trained for 200 200 k steps, J = 32 J{=}32 sampling steps, 512 512 samples, and the same GPT-2-large judge with the decoding and retokenization that we use everywhere else, and we report gen-PPL together with the unigram entropy H H of the same samples. Three policies recur throughout this section, and we define them once here. Commit- M M draws one component from the router at the all- [MASK] start, holds it for the whole trajectory, and returns that rollout without any selection at J J network calls. Best-of- M M runs one rollout per component and returns the argmin of the T = 4 T{=}4 Monte-Carlo mixture NELBO of Sec. 4.4 at M ⁡ ( J + T ) M(J{+}T) calls. Running evidence replaces that score with the log-probability that each component assigns to the tokens revealed along its own trajectory, which the trunk already computes at every step, and it therefore costs M ​ J MJ calls and no additional passes. Where two policies are compared on a fixed candidate pool, the per-step random stream is shared across the component rollouts, which removes the noise as a confounder. Under a shared stream and a frozen component, pruning never alters the trajectory of a surviving rollout. Hence, any pruning schedule can be evaluated from one complete run.

sections.heading: F.1 The gain is a property of the mixture
sections.text: We use two controls to separate the mixture from the reranking that decodes it. In the first control, which stays inside the model, the M M components are replaced by M M noise draws of one frozen component, while the budget, the selector and the judge are held fixed. As shown in Table 6 , this replacement costs 16 % 16\% at M = 4 M{=}4 ( 186 186 against 157 157 ) and 35 % 35\% at M = 8 M{=}8 ( 163 163 against 106 106 ). Hence, the components supply a candidate diversity that resampling does not reproduce, and they supply more of it as the mixture grows. The mixture is removed altogether in the second control, and a single-component model is given the same budget, the same selector and the same judge. Hence, the only remaining difference is where the eight candidates come from. We ran this control on two different single-component models, the first of which is our separately trained M = 1 M{=}1 checkpoint, which is MDLM by Proposition 4 and is matched to the M = 8 M{=}8 run in trunk, parameter count, corpus and 200 ​ k 200\text{k} -step budget. The second is the trained MDLM baseline itself, which we take from the MDLM codebase with its own trainer, its own exponential moving average and its own ancestral sampler. Each model draws eight i.i.d. chains with the same per-step seed offsets as the mixture arm and ranks them by its own T = 4 T{=}4 sequence ELBO at the identical 8 ​ ( J + T ) 8(J{+}T) calls. Every arm is scored and judged in a single process, which makes Table 7 a paired within-run comparison. Its mixture arm reaches 105.6 105.6 at J = 32 J{=}32 , reproducing the 105.6 105.6 of Table 10 and the 106 106 of Table 6 . sections.heading: Matching total calls rather than sequential steps.
sections.text: The comparison in Table 8 matches sequential depth, which is the axis that governs latency, and best-of- M M is ahead everywhere on that axis. A stricter comparison instead hands the single chain the whole parallel budget as extra steps. On LM1B, this changes nothing, because commit- M M at M = 8 M{=}8 saturates at 223.5 223.5 when it is given all 128 128 calls, whereas best-of- 8 8 at 16 16 steps spends the same 128 128 calls and reaches 169 169 . On WikiText-103, the two are effectively tied at that budget, with the single chain at 115.7 115.7 (entropy 5.33 5.33 ) against best-of- 8 8 at 118.9 118.9 . The gap reopens as the budget grows, and doubling it to 256 256 calls takes best-of- 8 8 to 75 75 at a sequential depth of only 32 32 steps, which the single chain does not approach even at four times its step count. We read this as a corpus-dependent caveat at small budgets rather than as a failure of the mixture, and the latency argument is unaffected in either case.

sections.text: The candidate pool in Table 10 is fixed to the one that the main results use, namely M M rollouts with one frozen component each and an independent noise stream per rollout, and the whole step grid is swept. sections.heading: F.4 The components span a quality-diversity frontier
sections.text: We report each component in isolation in Table 12 , both as a single rollout and as best-of- 8 8 draws from that component alone. The components are strongly heterogeneous, and their ordering is preserved across the two protocols up to a single adjacent swap at M = 8 M{=}8 and exactly at M = 4 M{=}4 . Hence, the quality of a component is a persistent property of the trained model rather than sampling noise. Reranking inside the strongest component reaches 47 47 , which is better than the mixture decode, but its unigram entropy falls to 4.42 4.42 against 4.96 4.96 for the mixture and roughly 5.6 5.6 for the data. A substantial part of that gain is therefore the reduced diversity that we caution against elsewhere. We read this as a frontier that the mixture acquires during training and that the choice of k k traverses at inference, with best-of- M M at the diverse end and single-component reranking at the high-fidelity end. Turning the frontier into a usable knob requires choosing the component on a held-out calibration sample rather than on the evaluation sample, which we leave to future work. sections.heading: Where the correlation lives.
sections.text: Probing a seven-point grid of ( t , s ) (t,s) pairs for the M = 16 M{=}16 model reveals that the latent does essentially all of its work at the very first unmasking step. The transition t = → 0.25 t{=}0\!\to\!0.25 already accounts for I ^ k ≈ 2.21 \widehat{\mathrm{I}}_{k}\approx 2.21 nats of the full transition’s ≈ 2.46 \approx 2.46 (seed means), whereas a late transition such as t = → 1.0 t{=}0.5\!\to\!1.0 captures essentially nothing ( 0.02 0.02 nats). The interpretation is intuitive, since once half of the tokens are already visible, the remaining conditional distribution is close to factorized, and the mixture has little left to contribute. Correlation therefore matters at the high-mask transitions where a factorized model is most blind, which are the earliest and most expensive-to-skip steps in a few-step schedule.

sections.heading: The router learns sixteen distinct modes.
sections.text: To check that the mixture has organized itself into the sixteen hidden values rather than collapsing, we freeze the latent to each fixed value in turn and measure the resulting sub-distribution. Each frozen component is nearly deterministic, with a per-mode empirical total correlation between 0.0 0.0 and 8.4 8.4 bits (most below 1 1 bit) and a correspondingly tiny unigram entropy, which is the signature of a component committed to a single hidden value, since conditioning on the hidden value removes almost all of the corpus’s correlation. The routed mixture over the sixteen components then reconstructs 26.7 26.7 of the 28 28 bits of total correlation, and shuffling the drawn k k across the batch leaves the mixture-level total correlation unchanged ( 26.6 26.6 bits), as expected once components are committed at draw time. Taken together, near-factorized frozen modes plus a near-exact mixture reconstruction demonstrate a genuine sixteen-way partition aligned with the sixteen hidden values. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.27529v1 [cs.LG] 29 Jul 2026 Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation Mansoor Ahmed \corresponding Yue-Tsz Fan Hemanth Venkateswara Murray Patterson \corresponding Abstract Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently . This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher’s quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively , and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M M factorized components tied by a single shared latent . Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M M . We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M = 1 M{=}1 . The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1 × 2.1\times to 3.3 × 3.3\times over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M M , and at M = 8 M{=}8 , it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git 1 Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA 2 Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA mahmed76@student.gsu.edu, mpatterson30@gsu.edu 1 Introduction Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models now rival autoregressive language models, as they fill every position of a sequence in parallel rather than one token at a time ( Potaptchik et al. 2026 ) . To keep a single denoising step cheap, they factorize the per-step transition across positions, p t → s ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) = ∏ i = 1 L p i ​ ( x s i ∣ x t ) , p_{t\to s}(x_{s}\mid x_{t})\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{i}(x_{s}^{i}\mid x_{t}), (1) and decide every token independently given the current sequence x t x_{t} ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) . This independence is what makes a step cheap, and it is also what makes few-step generation challenging when the target couples positions that must be decided together. If a sentence pairs a subject with a verb that must agree in number, or an opening bracket with its closing match, the correct tokens are correlated, and an independent update commits to them separately. A factorized step may match the individual token marginals, while assigning substantial probability to jointly inconsistent combinations, and additional denoising steps may therefore be needed to resolve the mismatch. Conditioned on k k , the positions remain independent, but each component concentrates on a consistent completion. Marginalizing k k preserves the same per-position marginals as in (a), while placing all joint mass on the agreement set. Thus, two rank-one components express the correlated completion in one transition. Currently, two model families dominate this trade-off. Likelihood models such as MDLM ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) and SEDD ( Lou et al. 2023 ) train a strong factorized denoiser from scratch and then spend many steps at inference, where the factorization assumption is least harmful. Few-step accelerators take a trained teacher and compress its many-step behaviour into a handful of steps, either by distillation (Di4C ( Hayakawa et al. 2024 ) , SDTT ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre 2025 ) ) or by coupling rectification (ReDi ( Yoo et al. 2026 ) ). Both methods are effective, but they inherit the teacher’s quality ceiling. It is well understood that a student cannot outrun the teacher it imitates ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) , and rectification degrades after a few rounds. Hence, neither family removes the factorization at its root. We ask whether correlated steps can be modeled natively without a teacher. Our answer is Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), whose finite-time kernel is a mixture of M M factorized components selected by a latent k ∈ [ M ] k\in[M] : Ψ t → s θ ​ ( x s ∣ x t ) = ∑ k = 1 M w k θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) ​ ∏ i = 1 L P i θ ​ ( x s i ∣ x t , k , t , s ) . \Psi^{\theta}_{t\to s}(x_{s}\mid x_{t})=\sum_{k=1}^{M}w^{\theta}_{k}(x_{t},t,s)\prod_{i=1}^{L}P^{\theta}_{i}(x_{s}^{i}\mid x_{t},k,t,s). (2) Conditioned on ( x t , t , s ) (x_{t},t,s) , we first sample k ∼ w ( ⋅ ∣ x t , t , s ) k\sim w(\cdot\mid x_{t},t,s) , and we then sample the coordinates of X s X_{s} independently given k k . Thus, k k couples positions after marginalization, while each component remains factorized. At M = 1 M{=}1 , LKF reduces to MDLM. This mechanism produces a teacher-free few-step gain. On the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks, the mixture learns heterogeneous components, and a best-of- M M decode that ranks those components by the model’s own likelihood turns them into a few-step gain. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We introduce a latent-kernel discrete flow-map (LKF) whose step is a mixture of M M factorized components tied by one shared latent. 2. We give an exact information decomposition of the correlation a rank- M M step can carry, turning the question of whether the latent captures correlation into two bounded, estimator-validated quantities. 3. We test LKF on synthetic datasets with closed-form total correlation (TC). A hidden-agreement dataset shows that the captured information and the held-out likelihood grow monotonically with M M , while a parity control shows that the latent provably cannot help. 4. We evaluate unconditional generation on the LM1B and WikiText-103 benchmarks against likelihood and accelerator models. At M = 8 M{=}8 , LKF improves few-step generative perplexity by roughly 3 × 3\times over the likelihood baselines and surpasses the distilled and rectified accelerators without using any teacher, with the gain growing with M M . 2 Related work Masked diffusion as likelihood models. Building on the absorbing D3PM process ( Austin et al. 2021 ) , MDLM ( Sahoo et al. 2024 ) shows that the absorbing evidence lower bound (ELBO) reduces to a weighted cross-entropy on masked positions under the SUBS parameterization, which zeroes the mask probability and copies revealed tokens through, and SEDD ( Lou et al. 2023 ) reaches comparable likelihoods by learning discrete score ratios for a continuous-time Markov chain ( Campbell et al. 2022 ) . Both are factorized per step, where a rate changes one coordinate at a time in SEDD, and the reverse kernel is a product over positions in MDLM. Hence, both need many evaluations before the sample quality saturates. LKF reduces to MDLM as its M = 1 M{=}1 special case (Proposition 4 ) by adding intra-step correlation. Few-step generation by distillation and rectification. SDTT ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre 2025 ) self-distills a masked model through time, and Di4C ( Hayakawa et al. 2024 ) distills into a mixture-of-products student, proving that factorized students face a Θ ⁡ ( 1 / J ) \Theta(1/J) total-variation floor. Hence, both methods are structurally teacher-bounded. ReDi ( Yoo et al. 2026 ) instead rectifies the source-to-target coupling, provably decreasing the same conditional total correlation per round, but its gains ride on a monotone entropy collapse. LKF asks the complementary question, whether the mixture structure can be trained from scratch with no teacher ceiling, enriching the kernel until the correlation is representable. Flow maps and from-scratch few-step models. Flow maps learn a finite-time transition kernel indexed by two times, where one network serves every step. Building on the discrete flow matching family ( Gat et al. 2024 ; Campbell et al. 2024 ) , Discrete Flow Maps ( Potaptchik et al. 2026 ) are the closest from-scratch sibling that carries correlation through position-dependent simplex schedules, but with no latent and no mixture. Concurrent theory quantifies the schedule-level tradeoff between total correlation and step count ( Dmitriev et al. 2026 ; Zhao and Cai 2026 ) , complementing our per-step accounting. LKF is a likelihood model and differs by making each jump a low-rank mixture of discrete-token kernels whose latent is explicit and measurable, a mechanism orthogonal to simplex schedules. 3 Preliminaries and background Setup. Starting from all- [MASK] , a learned transition removes a little corruption per step, where each step is one network forward pass (NFE). Masked diffusion. A monotone schedule κ t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \kappa_{t}\in[0,1] keeps each token independently with probability κ t \kappa_{t} and otherwise replaces it by [MASK] ( Austin et al. 2021 ) (Eq. ( 4 )). Masking is also called absorbing, where the reverse process turns [MASK] into real tokens. A denoiser takes the whole partially masked sequence and predicts a categorical over its clean value for each masked position, factorized across positions as in Eq. ( 1 ). Discrete flow and diffusion models come in two flavours. Each step forwards the trunk once, samples tokens at the currently masked positions from a single component k k under the analytic (cached) reverse update, and keeps already-revealed tokens fixed because masking is monotone (pseudocode in Appendix C ). Since the latent is tied to a whole sequence, a rollout draws k k once at the all- [MASK] start, where w w is a constant prior, and holds it for the entire trajectory. Every step is therefore explained by the same latent, and the decode matches the sequence-level semantics of the training objective. One such rollout uses a single component and therefore leaves the mixture’s heterogeneity unused. Our decode, best-of- M M , realizes that heterogeneity at inference by running all M M rollouts in parallel with one component frozen in each, scoring every finished candidate with the model’s own sequence-level mixture negative ELBO (NELBO) of Eq. 16 , and returning the argmin (Algorithm 2 in Appendix C ). The model’s own likelihood is used for selection, which needs no reward model, no external judge, and no teacher, and the M M rollouts are independent and therefore run concurrently at the sequential depth of a single chain. The scoring passes can in fact be reduced. Every step evaluates all M M components in order to marginalize over k k , which makes the log-probability that component k k assigns to the tokens revealed at that step available at no extra cost, and accumulating it along a trajectory gives a per-component running evidence by the time the rollout finishes. Selecting on this quantity is free and is at least as accurate as the Monte-Carlo NELBO. Since it ranks candidates before they finish, it also lets the weakest rollouts be pruned partway through, cutting the cost of best-of- M M by roughly a factor of three. 5 Theoretical analysis A mixture kernel ( Wang et al. 2026 ) captures the correlation . Limitations We note two main limitations of LKF. The first is that the single-step exactness is capped by the per-step factorization. Each step is factorized given ( x t , k ) (x_{t},k) , and one disagreeing token can therefore push a sample off support independently of M M , which only smaller steps or a richer per-step structure would remove. The second is that the learned router is not very informative along sampling trajectories.
